utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. Today we are Tuesday, the 27th of May, 2008. My greetings to the witness, the accused, the Defence teams, and the Prosecution, as well as all the people helping us in these proceedings. As regards to the decision that we were supposed to render this morning, since the Prosecutor told us yesterday that he was going to file submissions, we have decided not to render that decision this morning or today. We, of course, authorise the Prosecutor to file motions if he wishes to file any motions, and we will render a written decision and not an oral decision. A written decision will therefore be rendered. Mr. Stringer, you are going to file some submissions or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, we have not. I wasn't sure -- we weren't sure at the conclusion of yesterday's proceedings whether in fact we would be called upon to do that. I can consult with Mr. Scott, and I'm sure that we can file something swiftly. We can try to do that today so that the Trial Chamber can render a swift decision as well. But at the moment we have not written anything, but we can begin that process at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Since the decision with regard to the clarification of the decision that was rendered, I remind Mr. Karnavas that he has one hour and two minutes; and in compliance with the directive number 7, he now has one hour and two minutes for his direct examination and re-examination. And now for a few brief moments I would like to move into private session because I would like to address Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So I will now give the floor to Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Ambassador Sancevic. Okay. You're going to have to speak up now so that we can all hear you, and I will be asking you to keep your answers rather brief because of the time limitations. Now, if we could go back to the document where we left off yesterday, and with the usher's assistance that would be P 06454. And I'll be first going back to more or less where we left off on that page --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That will be page 45, Your Honours, in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- and in the Croatian version, we'll give you the ERN number. It's 01322935, 935. Do you have it, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, yesterday we left off where you had mentioned that you had been told from Mr. Arif Pasalic during the Turkish goodwill mission, the Turkish/Croatian goodwill mission about the intentions to go all the way to the sea. And I want to follow up a little bit where you continue to speak on page 45 where you say on the second paragraph towards the middle of -- after the first sentence you say: "So I think about the main body we must -- about the main body and these other situations, we must somehow make it clear that our policy is a sort of symbiosis. It's a symbiosis to save the people, to save indigenous in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, the Croats, but at the same time the strategic importance of the main body of Bosnia and Herzegovina because it's a matter of south Croatia's survival." And then we see later on, you talk about Muslim fundamentalism. But could you please explain to us what exactly you meant by that, that it's -- that you wanted to -- about the strategic importance of the main body of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we look at the map, we can see clearly that the lower part of Croatia is very narrow, and that is the territory of what was formerly the autonomous, the independent, republic of Dubrovnik. It would be only natural for the hinterland to be in some way connected with that narrow strip. Strategically and militarily speaking, such a narrow strip cannot be defended in any way. It's hard to speak of any sort of defence there. When Croatia wanted to liberate that area from the greater Serbs, in view of the fact that Dubrovnik was encircled, I had to ask from Mr. Akmadzic, the Bosnian government, to allow the Croatian troops to enter into that narrow area just beyond the proper Croatian territory simply because it was a strategically important area. I was granted that permission, and every time the Croatian army had to enter that area an agreement had to be reached with the Bosnian government first. I received permission from Mr. Akmadzic, who was the then-prime minister of the Bosnian government, for the Croatian troops to enter that part of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina with a view to liberating the Dubrovnik coastal area. The importance of that action is evident from what Arif Pasalic said, and I mean the action of liberating Dubrovnik. And when I'm referring to Arif Pasalic, I'm not referring to the Bosnian government. We had good relations with the Bosnian government, but there were some extremist elements who wanted to cut off that area of what was formerly the Dubrovnik republic in order to set up, develop extremist ties between Bosnian Muslims and pan-Islamic - and I mean extremist pan-Islamic - elements abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we could go -- and to fuller understand your explanation, if we could go back to page 39 in the same document, and for you it would be page -- the last two digits -- the last three digits are 929, 929. And it's 39 for the rest of us. And let me just read a portion of this. You start by saying the ambassador of the Republic of Croatia in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then you say, "The constant of our policy and your policy was saving people. There is a constant thread to humaneness. However, our policy so far was generally of a global nature. "However, besides this thread that is constantly present, our policy with regard to Bosnia and Herzegovina - I'm speaking about the policy of the Republic of Croatia and our leadership - was fairly global." Then you go on to say: "However, we move forward. We can see that all these problems in Bosnia-Herzegovina cannot be resolved in a global and different way because a situation has been created where de facto each enclave has its own specific problem, and therefore, a kind of classification of the various situations in Bosnia and Herzegovina should somehow be made." And then you say: "We have the main body, which is the Croatian republic of Herceg-Bosna, a compact part of the Croatian republic of Herceg-Bosna, because it is assumed that the Croatian republic of Herceg-Bosna includes that it actually has no borders. That has been established already in the constitutional idea. "However, the part in Western Herzegovina, Livno, Duvno, et cetera, the situation in that compact Croatian part is quite different from the one in Central Bosnia and Northern Bosnia, generalising about it in a way because in the situation in Central Bosnia and Northern Bosnia, we have different situations. "What I would call the main body of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which was a hybrid. It was the HDZ, Croatian Democratic Union, grassroots, then civilian HDO" -- should be HVO -- "military, was built on that, and the formation process is still in progress. In addition to all these things, we have seen in Croatia proper the accompany the creation of government. "We are all aware that when government is not fully established or perfected or refined, there are all sorts of things. People say smuggling, crime, this and that. Here's just an example." And then you go on to say: "For instance, we have managed - I mean the Croats - in the main part, for instance, managed to set up the detention camps ..." Now, I understand it with regard to the word "set up," you've indicated at least to me during the proofing session that that's not how it should be translated. Do you want to comment on that part before I continue reading?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to say for a fact that I never used the term "formirati," set up, but rather "rasformirati," meaning to disband the detention camps, and I should like this to be corrected because this is a glaring mistake, which among other things is quite illogical because at that point the prisons were either in the process of being disbanded or had already been disbanded by that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know quite a lot about the disbandment of Croat prisons, although I know that at the time Muslim prisons were being disbanded as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Sancevic, that's enough. I really need to get going, but thank you for that clarification. Therefore -- and then you go on. I'm going to the next page. This is page 41 -- it will be the next page -- I'll keep reading. I'll skip part of that last paragraph. You go on to say: "Therefore, another formation is underway there. Let's have a quick look at Central Bosnia. We have two tendencies. One is the resistance of the Zepce enclaves. We have just been there, and that thing is present in Vares, et cetera. "However, there is de facto the tendency that you mentioned, Mr. President, to adopt to the Muslim republic. "The people who see they have no chance to survive in that area try to look for ways to ... Komsic is there, too; the archbishop is there, too, and all other variations of those tendencies. "The problem is that each of those tendencies - except Komsic, who was in contact with you - in a way, in its own way wants to accommodate, to lean towards the Muslims. "That's why I don't know. I would not agree with the prime minister because in the enclaves in Central Bosnia we have very different situations. Take only Zepce and Usora, Orasje, Brcko, Tuzla, et cetera. "The thing is that it's not under our control. None of those tendencies to save, accommodate, et cetera, are under our control, unfortunately." Then I'll skip the next paragraph. Then you say: "We should study a little bit the situation in these different enclaves and see, for example, Zepce. You mention that the protection and fight for Zepce must be established somehow through the Serbian side. "However, in the case of Usura, there is already some sort of connection with the Muslims. "However, we cannot let them - for example, in the case of the Muslims and in the case of Zepce - roll on their own vis-a-vis the Serbs and vis-a-vis the Muslims. We must somehow approach each side and secure the existence of those enclaves because if that continues to roll on like this, we will lose all the enclaves." Now, having read this portion, Ambassador Sancevic, could you please explain to us what you were trying to convey in the context in which this conversation was going on? What were you conveying to the group, including President Izetbegovic -- President Tudjman at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The gist of what I said at the meeting was that the situations within Bosnia and Herzegovina differ from location to location. As far as the Croatian situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina or the situation involving Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina is concerned, one had to make a distinction between the situation in Bosnia, where they were enclaves, unlike Western Herzegovina which was a compact area. What needs stressing is that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna had never set up or established any borders. There wasn't even a possibility for it to do that because in some areas there was mixed population, just as was the case in Bosnia, northern and central, and in other areas there was mono-ethnic population. The very make-up of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was not defined geographically, and what I'm telling here to President Tudjman is that we need to clearly define the different situations in order to find adequate remedies for them. Some of the enclaves were surrounded by greater Serbs, others by Muslims, and still others by both these parties. What this meant for the Croatian policy toward Bosnia-Herzegovina was that it was faced with a very complex situation. It wasn't the same if you talked of Zepce, Tuzla, Orasje. Every enclave entailed its own difficulties and had to be discussed and regarded separately. What was more, the situations tended to change very frequently, and they had to be constantly analysed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's see if we go -- sticking with the same transcript now, if we could move to page 81 because now, based on this -- on your briefing and what you have indicated earlier, now we see what President Tudjman says. It's page 81, and in the Croatian version - I'll get you right now - the last three digits are 971, 971.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would have -- with your permission, Mr. Karnavas, I would have had a question to the previous passage from which you have read, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, you have spoken about the camps and the disbanding of the camp, and then it is in the English version on page 41, you speak of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in that main body, and it says there are almost none, camps; because it was like a family, it functioned like a family. Could you expand on that? What did you mean when you said that this functioned like a family in connection with, I suppose, Dretelj, Gabela, Ljubuski, Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me explain the following. When one declaratorial government disappeared - that was Tito's authority - with the disappearance of that authority, there ensued a period of complete anarchy. Now, in Western Herzegovina, at some point prisons disappeared; there were none to be found. Now, I was an on-looker as a representative of Croatia in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and what I'm telling you now is what was my understanding of what I observed. I never addressed directly the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. This was something that I observed, that there were no more prisons there. Then somebody created a scandal in Medjugorje. There was a soldier - how should I put it? - he was a -- I don't know how you call it. He was a Briton who was a mercenary, basically, and he fought in the Muslim forces. He showed up in front of the embassy and made a display there. Then I asked the police of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna to take the gentleman away. What happened next? They took him to the police station, and there having been no prisons they released him after he was kept there for an hour. I'm telling you this merely to illustrate the fact that there were no prisons. With the breaking out of the conflict and in the absence of proper prisons, there had to be set up certain locations where prisoners could be held. Thus, such detention centres or prisons were set up on both the Muslim and Croat sides, like the ones you had around Mostar, the ones in Central Bosnia. These were makeshift locations in view of the conflicts that broke out between extremist Muslims and extremist Croats and not between all Muslims and Croats. I don't know if I was explicit enough, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll leave it at that. We could go on at length probably, but that's not the purpose, and I do not want to take away any -- I'm not taking your time, anyway, Mr. Karnavas --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- you're well aware that I do not want it to become late. Thank you. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, going back to what we were talking about, the portion that I just read, now if we go back to the page that I asked you to look at, which in English is page 81, and this is page -- the last three digits 971 of the transcript, let's see what President Tudjman responds in relation to what you have indicated earlier. And I'm going to start in the middle of the page. He says: "Or, it seems to me that we could this, I have it, Sancevic raised it here. There is aside from the state leadership and the political leadership and the military leadership of the Croatian Republic Herceg-Bosna, we must a position -- a political representation of the Union of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I mean, what is outside -- let's not kid ourselves. What is, I mean, outside the Croatian republic. "I think it might even be called the Croatian Council of the Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and let's envision that. And, I mean, that this political representation of that part of the Croatian people, the Croatian people which is outside the Republic objectively, should include, apart from the HDZ, Croatian Democratic Union, people like Komsic and some others. "Thus, to knock out the arguments, both malicious and politicking, that we are not taking care of Croatian people in Sarajevo, in Vares, Zepce, and so on. So we have to take our stand on this ..." Now, Ambassador Sancevic, did you understand what President Tudjman was saying in response to what you had raised earlier?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now we are talking about the Vance-Owen proposal, which didn't go through. Actually, it was modified, this proposal dealing with the crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina and resulted in the Owen-Stoltenberg proposal, which talks about the union of Bosnia-Herzegovina and its republics. This is actually Owen-Stoltenberg's plan. Since they did not manage to win over Serbia or even a large portion of Muslims in favour of Vance-Owen plan, now we are dealing with Owen-Stoltenberg's plan, which envisages Bosnia-Herzegovina as a union of republics or a federation of three different republics, and this is just a matter of different terminology that I'm using. And President Tudjman said this: This is an entirely new ball game, and we had to think how to organize or start organizing or how to face this new situation when we're dealing with three units, three entities, which were even given the titles of republics, but we are still dealing with the proposal for a federation. Obviously, what was always present there was the fact that a future possible Republika Srpska must adjust itself to this new federation and that -- yes, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you here. Here President Tudjman is talking about a Croatian council, and he mentions places such as Sarajevo, Vares, Zepce, and so on. Very quickly, why is President Tudjman making this proposal in light of what you said earlier because you said Sancevic raised this here, and what you had raised earlier was that you have these three different situations or variations in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So why is President Tudjman now recommending a Croatian council, and he's mentioning people like Komsic, Sarajevo, Zepce, and what have you. Just very briefly if you know; if not, I'll move on. My time is very limited, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can give you a perfect explanation for that. President Tudjman actually said it clearly and expressed it clearly in his ideas as to how to support the plans of the international Vance-Owen and Stoltenberg's plans, and he also had in mind the situation among the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina. There was a very strong intellectual -- group of intellectuals, Croats, in Sarajevo, and Mr. Komsic was one of them. On behalf of that group, Mr. Komsic went to see Mr. Tudjman and talked to him, asking him to take into account a kind of opposition among the Croats in context with the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then he asked me to get in touch with the group and to try and see what their problems were. As I've already told you, every enclave had its own problems, and this included Sarajevo as well. Sarajevo also had its own problems, and he wanted me in my capacity as the ambassador of Croatia to get in touch with these people in Sarajevo because I did go to Sarajevo from time to time, and he asked me to see what these people wanted, what they had in mind --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You're not answering my question, and I have very little time. Why is President Tudjman suggesting the establishment of a Croatian council, keeping in mind that he's interested in the Komsic -- the Croats in Sarajevo, Vares, Zepce, and so on, and not only the Herzegovinians. Could you please explain that in one minute; if not, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I keep on emphasizing the difference between the situation of Croats in Bosnia as opposed to the situation of Croats in Herzegovina. Dr. Tudjman actually tried in every possible case to achieve a symbiosis in his position towards the both because it was in his best interest to please not only the Croats in Herzegovina but also the Croats in Sarajevo, Sarajevo in Central Bosnia, Croats in northern Bosnia and the enclaves and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could move on to 1D 02911 -- 1D 02991. This is a presidential transcript, 13 February 1994, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, is that 2991 or 291 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 2911. 2911. In incidentally, for the record -- while we're at it, looking for this, because I was a little taken aback by the comments made by the Prosecutor back on May 12, 19 -- 2008. Pursuant to the Court's order, we did file a list of our exhibits, and in that list we filed the previous exhibit, which was the presidential transcript, P 06454, where Ambassador Sancevic's name is highlighted there and -- whereas I indicated yesterday, the portions with respect to the objectionable part by the Prosecution where they were claiming somehow that we had introduced something that was not already presented to them as part of our case. You can see clearly, here they were noticed well in advance, their transcript, which was transcript provided by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can respond if the Trial Chamber wants to continue to beat this dead horse, as we say, and -- where I come from. But I'm just going to note for the record that the Trial Chamber ruled that, in fact, the issue raised was outside the scope of all the notice, the summaries, and that no proofing note had been given and that it excluded a rule that Defence could not go into the issue. So that's the record, and I'm not going to engage in any further debates with counsel on this issue. The record says what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I merely pointed it out, Your Honours, because yesterday the Prosecutor said that there are all these documents and they can't be asked to look for them and they can't be -- you know, we're supposed to be prepared. As I indicated yesterday, they drafted the indictment. We're using their document. It's in the document. We highlighted this information to them two weeks ago, and for them to claim somehow that this Defence team has not taken the moral high ground, I find it rather disingenuous, and that's what I'm pointing out for the record, that they can't on the one hand dump all this information on us, and then when we try to use their information against them, they claim foul. That's all I'm saying. They were noticed. Going back to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll respond if you want me to respond; if you don't need to hear from me, then I'll just allow counsel to proceed. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Again, I don't think it's useful for any party to claim the moral high ground, nor do I think it's useful for any party to claim that another's been disingenuous. The fact is the testimony about the meeting with General Pasalic was not disclosed to us in advance. The trial -- the transcripts contain many discussions of many, many things, and I don't think any party ought to be expected to search for the needle in the haystack in the absence of sufficient notice that a specific issue will be covered, as the Trial Chamber's ruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's rather rich, but I've been claiming in fact the very same. We've been getting the haystack all along. So in any event, I'll move on, Mr. President, but I found that rather rich.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What they've been getting are proofing notes promptly from the Prosecution throughout the course of the proofing sessions even if it means proofing notes are provided over the course of the weekend. I was receiving -- Mr. Karnavas knows how to get in touch with me. There was no proofing note on this, and it was in fact an ambush, and he's trying to make it other than what it truly was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you are going to deal with the presidential transcript number 2911. I have no idea what question you are about to put to the witness. Let's wait and see. Please put your question to the witness, and then things will become clearer. The Prosecutor seems to believe that you will raise issues not outlined in the summary. I have no idea. Let's listen to your question, and then we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. If we go to page 53, we will see that towards the latter part of the page we have the gentleman's name, our witness's name, Dr. Sancevic; and, of course, two weeks ago we noted that we would be using this transcript, and we pointed out that he was one of the participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Here, Ambassador Sancevic, you say - and I'll just quote part of the transcript - "whenever we discuss these problems, we always fall for Salajdzic. Anything that Salajdzic says about these two" -- okay. I'm sorry. The page -- your page is 501. I'm sorry. 501. Those are the last three digits. I apologise for not getting the number to you. 501. You will see your name there. And then you go on to say: "Anything that Salajdzic says about these two republics somehow boils down to the idea that Croatia should carry all western-oriented Muslims to the west on her shoulders, so to speak, because Europe would find it agreeable. However, we have mentioned today that there are two -- that there are factions. There is Ganic's faction; there is the Mujahadin faction, et cetera. One of the objectives of this faction. The Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina have two options," and then, of course, I'm going to move on to another section, and I'm going to go to page 57 before I pose my question. So if you look to -- skip a couple of pages and you go to page 505 in your transcript, 505, you will see the very last sentence you say: "Then Mufti from Mostar gave a speech in Berlin at a Mujahadin meeting and said that the time has come for Islam to conquer Europe." President Tudjman asks you: "Was that now, recently?" And you respond: "Just over a year ago." Then you go on later on in that passage to talk about Izetbegovic's wish to get to the sea and that it was not for them to swim or unload goods, similar to what we discussed yesterday. And then if we go to page 58, so that will be the next page for you somewhere, you say - and I'm going to pick it up in the middle of the paragraph: "I think that in the general context of all of this if you put this forward and the suggestions you made in Bonn - three republics, a border - and what we have heard from these Muslims, then it would appear far more acceptable to the Western world once they become aware of a different and terrible possibility which could become reality. We are not making threats but only explaining things." Then the president -- I'm going to -- you go on, but I'm going to skip. Then the president says to you: "Nevertheless, Zdravko, would a union of two republics with clearly defined borders be a more acceptable solution to you?" And you say: "Yes, if we can at least be in some way turned towards the west, and this Sarajevo matter, taking your suggestion as a starting point, these are the first steps, you know, as well as setting up a border, regardless of whether it is a hard border or a soft one." Now, we can all read this transcript, but basically could you please tell us, what exactly was this conversation about?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, generally speaking, there was a desire on the part of the international community for the group of Muslims who were in favour of the European option and who adopted all the European elements to follow the Republic of Croatia in its footsteps towards Europe. On the other hand, there was another group, the so-called extremist group, which was opposed to the accession of the first Muslim group to Europe. Their attitude was that of war-mongerers. One of them was Mr. Smajkic, whom I saw in the video-clip, who was in favour of conquering Europe. His position was extremist. All I'm saying is that in Bosnia-Herzegovina there were always Muslims who were in favour of Europe and there were also extremists, but not always. Only recently the latter group appeared. It was only when Marsal Tito became the leader of the third world. He opened or paved the way for the Muslim religious leaders to go to various universities, and many of them who had been educated at various universities adopted the extremist Islam ideas there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And when you --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- just like Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may, just one small point. You said recently. They appeared recently. What did you refer to date-wise?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What do you mean by recently?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm asking the witness .

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In what context because the witness will be confused. If you could point out the context. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's page 20, the second line. All I'm saying is there were always -- Muslims -- it was only when Marsal Tito became the leader -- only recently the latter group appeared, 22, 23, the extremists, Muslim extremists. What did you refer to when you say "recently"? From which point back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Recently meaning that the pro-European line among Muslims existed back in the Austro-Hungarian period starting with 1878, whereas the extremist tendencies only appeared when the Muslim imams in Bosnia-Herzegovina were allowed to continue education at various universities and happened during the time when Marsal Tito was the leader of the third world. They were sent to various universities where they were educated and where they studied the extremist Islam positions, just like Smajkic did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So that would mean several years ago, before 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. Yes. You're correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And when there's that reference about two republics, is that the reference with respect to the Federation as opposed to having a -- the federation with Republika Srpska, the two entities, as opposed to what was previously on the table, three republics?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. That's a leading question --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll withdraw. If he has read the transcript, which -- it's self-evident what the discussion is about, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about Bonn? There was a reference to the Bonn conference. Do you know anything about that, very quickly? The portion that I read to you, it said something about the president had been to Bonn.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. After a certain time, he went to Bonn to talk to Mr. Cole.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And do you know, based on you being one of the insiders, so to speak, given that you were the ambassador to Bosnia-Herzegovina, do you know what if anything was discussed at Bonn? And I'm talking about in relation to what -- the portion that we just read in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. I was not there, but I know from the subsequent comments that one of the things that was highlighted in Bonn was the fact that there were some Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina; there were still a large number of Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina, who were in favour of Europe and with whom we had to, in one way or another, strive towards helping these Muslims acceding the future European Union, and so on and so forth. The entire situation revolved around that. The fact was that we could not classify all the Muslims the same and call them the same because there were -- there was one kind of Muslims, and there was another kind of Muslims, and this is why I keep on insisting on defining exactly which Croats, which Muslims, which greater Serbs, which Serbs generally. You've noticed that I am using the term "greater Serbs" because we cannot use the one and only national term on all the various fractions of that particular nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, we're going to move on to some -- we're going to leave the presidential transcripts alone, and we're going to move to some documents very quickly because I have very limited time. 1D 02394, 1D 02394. Okay, do you have the document, sir? Do you have it, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] 2394?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. We see here from this document, it's dated 16th September 1993, and it's to the president of the Mesihat of the Islamic community for the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Slovenia, and we see that at the second page it's signed by Dr. Muhamed Alic. And just starting up with the very first paragraph: "On September 15th, 1993, MDS representatives, Dr. Ismet Hadziosmanovic, and Dr. Muhamed Alic visited his Highness, the bishop, at his residence in order to discuss the fate of the nuns and the friars detained in Konjic." Do you see that? You're shaking your head, sir. I need an answer. Please, you have to work with me.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well, yeah --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Yesterday, we looked at a particular transcript, and just for the record, it's 1D 02930. You don't need to look at it, but yesterday that's the transcript where we had Gojko Susak saying to Alija Izetbegovic that he had five planes full of goods sitting in Zagreb and that unless the situation in Konjic was solved he would not get a single bullet, and that was on page 26 of that particular transcript. Now -- and this was, by the way, the transcript was 27 March 1993. Now, when Gojko Susak was talking about the situation in Konjic back in March of 1993, was he referring to what we see here being resolved to some extent or still unresolved, in a sense, as of 16th September 1993, the freeing up of the nuns and friars that were being held by the Muslim leadership or whoever was holding them?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were held by extremist Muslims. Precisely in this document, we have pro-European Muslims, Dr. Hadzihasanovic, whom I know, and Dr. Alic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Hadziosmanovic. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And there we have the instance where pro-European Muslims are intervening on behalf of the nuns and friars who are supposed to be released. I'm emphasizing the difference between the pro-European Muslims, with whom I had pretty close ties; Dr. Ismet Hadziosmanovic; Dr. Muhamed Alic. At some point, President Tudjman suggested that they become members of the Government of Herceg-Bosna. Please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. I just want to make sure that we confirm because back in March, you've got Gojko Susak talking to the president of the presidency Izetbegovic about the situation in Konjic. Here we have a letter, 16 September 1993, talking about nuns and friars from Konjic. Are we talking about the same situation?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the same situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we go on to the next document, 1D 02275.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it. 0275.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: While we're looking for that document, I trust on the previous document it has been -- that the Trial Chamber will focus on the last paragraph in the first page where we talk about -- it talks about a Mr. Vlado Maric, an engineer who has been performing the function of a technical director of Jablanica water-plant, that they also are looking for his release. I only mention this because of the issue of water that has come up in the previous -- through previous witnesses on the Prosecution's case. Now, directing your attention at 1D 02275, we see that this is a declaration on the implementation of the Washington Agreement. Do you see it, sir? Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 2275? Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now if we look towards the bottom of the page, the third paragraph from the bottom, it says: "Expressing their irrevocable support to the implementation of the Washington Agreement on the establishment of the Federation as well as its confederal linking of the Republic of Croatia ..." Let me stop right there. Yesterday we talked a little bit about confederation. Is this the same concept that is being talked about here, the one that was earlier raised early on?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And I think if we look at the second page, towards the bottom it says: "Confirming their interests in the urgent implementation of the aforementioned principles declaration agreement has been reached on. "Widening and strengthening of the defence cooperation on the basis of the Agreement on Friendship and Cooperation" -- I underscore that for the Trial Chamber's attention since we've been mentioning this in the past -- "between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina of July 21, 1992." Again, I underscore that. And so -- and this is now July 22nd, 1995. So we see, sir, do we not, that part of the Washington Agreement -- part of this declaration, which is in furtherance of the Washington Agreement, is tying in and making reference to the Agreement on Friendship and Cooperation that dated back to July 21st, 1992, and we see a continuity; do we not, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. It's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What was the purpose of it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, throughout the period from 1991 to 1995 there was present this idea of a rapprochement between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Washington Agreement was the ultimate symbiosis or the ultimate achievement of that effort. The early days of that effort can be summed up on that agreement on the friendship and close ties between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I relied upon it all the way until the signing of the Washington Agreement. The Washington Agreement then provided me with another valuable document in that process of coming closer to -- in this process of Croatia's rapprochement with Bosnia-Herzegovina and its development of cooperation with that country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go on -- well, before we go on to the next document, I just want to preface my question with what we heard yesterday. You had indicated to us that you had participated in several meetings with President Tudjman, either tete-a-tete or meetings where he was presiding over various groups; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it's my understanding also that you had opportunities to hear Dr. Tudjman on numerous occasions when he delivered speeches as well?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I followed all the speeches delivered by President Tudjman. There were those that had -- of those that had to do with Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were 38, and this is only in one book that contains speeches, and I was of course present at some of these speeches --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Ambassador Sancevic, please let me lead you so I can finish because I'm going to run out of time and I won't be able to get this information. To cut to the quick, at some point you wrote a book, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What year was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's look at 1D 02339, 1D 02339. And it says over here, an insight into Bosnia. I take it that's the -- and then it says: "Notes of an ambassador. Croatian national policy towards BiH." Was this from your book?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] That is from my book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's my book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'm not going to discuss it because we can all read it, but I just want to focus you on the page, and it's not paginated, but if you look at the bottom of the page --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: On the English version, Your Honours, it would be 1D 52-0609.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And for you it's 0400, 0400, 4 00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please assist us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 4 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We can see in this chapter that you make references to two particular speeches that were given by Dr. Tudjman, but then you go on to say, at the bottom you say: "When we had this speech, also many numerous of the speeches of Croatian national policy of Dr. Tudjman towards BiH, I used them to create for my own needs a synthesis of the main elements of the Croatian national policy, but without listing them by some priorities or in particular order, because in given occasions and circumstances (scenarios) some elements were more important, but all were the constant of the Croatian national policy towards BiH." Now, sir, I'm going to go through these, and we see -- not all of them, but one says: "Preservation of BiH as an independent, integral, and friendly state." Was that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All this time, not only President Tudjman but the Croatian state policy in general - although, of course, the president of the republic did have great bearing on that policy - never called into question the existence of Bosnia-Herzegovina as an independent sovereign state. This was in the interests of the Croatian people and the Croatian government, and I acted accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And you talk about -- that it should be a federal organization, the equality of three constituent nations through federal organization. That's what we talked about yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I respond briefly?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The federal organization comes from Mr. Ahtissari back in 1991 when it was accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since then Cutileiro, Vance-Owen, and Owen-Stoltenberg, and the Contact Group and the Washington Agreement, all of it was in the service of the Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And then you -- further down on one of the lists you say: "A confederative alliance of the Republic of Croatia with federalized BiH, FBiH territorial, and just as possible distribution of BiH territories into federal entities, provinces, counties, cantons, with national attributes." That was your understanding, right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then, of course, because it was touched upon yesterday, and I believe it came with one of the questions, you say further down: "Protection of municipalities/enclaves of minority population in federal entity with minority [sic] nation attributes in that federal entity through redefinition of the territories of municipalities and by establishment of local self-management that would protect the population in the municipality/enclave and ensure its rights ..." That's what you meant when you were addressing one of the questions - and I believe it was from Judge Trechsel - yesterday, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I prefaced my questioning on this with that you had -- aside from having participated in meetings with Dr. Tudjman, that you had made references to his speeches and his writings. So just very briefly, if I could focus your attention on 1D 00401, and I'm just going to ask you one or two questions on this. 1D 0401. We see this is a text by Dr. Franjo Tudjman. It's on nationalism in contemporary Europe. Did you draw on his writings even well before or before the conflict or the break-up in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. When it comes to the view of Bosnia-Herzegovina and how it should be structured and as to the future ties between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia, on these matters I followed the policy which -- well, you have to know that President Tudjman read the book written by my father; and after all, I spoke to him directly. At times, these conversations lasted several hours, and we were discussing these problems. I know exactly what the intention was and what the Croatian state policy was vis-a-vis Bosnia-Herzegovina in the period between 1991 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. What my question -- my question was, Dr. -- Ambassador Sancevic: Did you draw upon Dr. Tudjman's writings prior to the events in order to understand President Tudjman and to write about what his intentions were? I'm asking the question: Did you refer to any of his writings prior to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And would this be one of them, one of the texts that he wrote: "Nationalism In Contemporary Europe"?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we look at the next document, 1D 02887, and I apologise for having to rush you through this, but we are labouring under some extreme difficulties with time. I'm just going to ask you one question. This is a book by Dr. Franjo Tudjman, 1D 02887. It's published in 1993. It is titled: "It Is Known: HDZ and the Struggle for Independence of Croatia."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know that I'm running out of time, but if I could have until 9.30 [sic], the end of the session, I think I could finish up everything, and I might even be finished before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You mean 10.30, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 10.30, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. This is a -- you're familiar with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you have as much time as you like. If you want to spend hours with this witness, that's your problem, but you -- a certain amount of time has been allocated to you for all your witnesses. You are the one who decides which -- how much time you will spend with each witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Perhaps I must say that I'm not quite of this opinion. I think agreed on four hours. You had proposed them, but you have until 10.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. It is kind of an inexact science.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1D 02887. Are you familiar with this textbook by Dr. Franjo Tudjman, the document itself? Okay, if you could look at 1D 02887.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] 2887, I have in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have before me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as I understand it, in this text there are various speeches that were given by Dr. Franjo Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in some of those speeches that are contained in this particular document, you were actually present when they were delivered?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] That's right. [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. It's my understanding that these are some of the writings, some of the speeches that you also relied on in addition to your meetings with Dr. Tudjman, you participating in meetings in drawing your conclusions which we read previously from your textbook, An Insight Into Bosnia --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I know counsel is under time pressure, but I'm going to object to leading questions of this nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is a looping question. I first established the foundation. That's where I went first. He's already indicated that. So I'm merely reemphasizing the fact that he had meetings; he met with Tudjman; he read his speeches; he participated in all sorts of other meetings; and he drew some conclusions. So while it may sound leading, in fact, it isn't leading. I'm merely building up on it. It's usually on cross-examination, but I think it needs to be done before professional Judges here in this courtroom, and it has been done, and I draw the attention to the gentleman -- to the Kordic trial where Judge May insisted on that sort of questioning in order to save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, did you refer to these speeches at all in formulating your own opinion as far as what the policy was?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Objection. Could we have a foundation in terms of which speeches the witness is being referred to? Every speech? Is it the entire -- are we offering the entire book into evidence on the basis of a few words from this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Again, we selected portions of this book. They were provided to the Prosecutor. It's under 1D 02887. Now, the gentleman -- I don't want to get personal, but the gentleman has been in court for the last two weeks, three weeks, while his other counterpart was doing all the labour with the other witnesses. I assume that the gentleman looked through our documents and he could see very well that these are speeches, some of them are only two or three lines, others are two or three pages. These are various speeches. They're numbered -- or dated, I should say. And I asked the question whether he was present or read them and -- as a basis for formulating his opinion as to what the policy was, in addition to his own participation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, if counsel's saying, which he hasn't said yet, and we haven't heard from the witness on this -- what the witness is talking about is the book, which is a huge tome. Now, if counsel is intending to direct the witness more specifically to the excerpts that he has in mind, that's fine, but I don't think that he's gotten there in his direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, if I was the one conducting this, I would have resolved the matter the following way. I would have asked the following question to the witness: Witness, have you read the books written by Mr. Tudjman? Answer: Yes, no. If the witness says no -- says yes, you can ask him which books he has read, and he will tell you: Such and such book published on such and such dates. Then you would ask him: Please have a look at this document, such and such paragraph. Then you would put your question to the witness, and the witness would answer, and there would be no objections. I know that you're trying to go quickly, but the Prosecution, of course, is going to react every time there is a leading question. But by resorting to very quick questions, you can lay the foundation and then ask your question without encountering any difficulties. Mr. Karnavas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Ambassador Sancevic, looking at 1D 02887, if we flip over to the page where it says: "Speech of President of the Republic of Croatia, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, at the 46th Session of the UN General Assembly of New York, May 22nd, 1992." That would be the very first speech, the very first speech. Did you read this speech? I will now demonstrate how long it will take to do that as opposed to asking --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, if we go to the next one, the next page, "Speech of the President of the Republic of Croatia Dr. Franjo Tudjman to the House of Representatives of the Croatian parliament on September 8th, 1992," page 11. Did you read this or were you present when this speech was delivered?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there and I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go to the next page, "Speech of the President of the Republic of Croatia, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, at the 47th Session of the UN General Assembly, New York, September 22nd, 1992." That's on page 14. Were you present or did you read this speech by Dr. Franjo Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there, but I read it carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Next page: "Speech of President of the Republic of Croatia, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, on the occasion of the parade of the Croatian army and navy in Dubrovnik, October 22nd, 1992." Were you present or did you read this speech by Dr. Franjo Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there, but I studied the speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, next page: Speech of the President of the Republic of Croatia, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, during the election campaign in Pazin, January 31, 1993." Were you present? That would be on page --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there, but I read the speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right after it was issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we go to the next page: "Speech of the parliament of the Republic of Croatia, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, during the election campaign of Pula, January 31, 1993." Were you present there, or did you read this speech?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there, but I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at the last one, next one: "Speech of the President of the Republic of Croatia, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, on the joint session of the House of the Croatian Parliament of March 23, 1993." Were you present, or did you read this?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And this will be -- time doesn't permit us, but I do draw the attention of the Court on the last part of page -- of the first page and the first part of the second page. There is some interesting information there, but time does not allow us to discuss the document. Next one: "Speech of the President of the Republic of Croatia Dr. Franjo Tudjman, on the session of PEN, at PEN Congress in Hvar," -- this is an island, for those of us who may not know -- "April 25, 1993." Were you present, or did you read this speech? It's a rather lengthy one.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there, and I read the speech, and I commented on it with President Tudjman afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, without reading the remainder of this, just to make the point, did you read all of his speeches, all of Dr. Franjo's speeches, that were contained in this particular document that I'm presenting to you, 1D 02887?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I make a small correction? There were five books, and what was extracted here were speeches out of five tomes because we were only referring and presenting the speeches by President Tudjman relating to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And can I ask --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: My -- okay. May I ask: Did you read all the speeches that are in this particular document that come from book 2?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you read all five volumes?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If we go on to the next document, 1D 02806. This is another book by Dr. Tudjman, "Croatian Word To the World." Have you read this book? There are talks or interviews --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Into -- these were interviews given to foreign representatives and journalists, and there are fewer texts relating to Bosnia-Herzegovina compared to the earlier speeches.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And again, let me ask again because there was an objection by the Prosecutor, and we were instructed how to do this by the Trial Chamber. Let me just ask this again: Did you refer to these sorts of speeches and documents in addition to everything else that you told us, the meetings and what have you, in drawing your conclusions as to what was the policy of the Republic of Croatia towards Bosnia-Herzegovina while you were in situ as the ambassador to Bosnia-Herzegovina for the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. I followed closely all the speeches by President Tudjman --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and I also had meetings with President Tudjman as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I just need to show -- just to round up and finish three quick documents, 1D 02927, and you can look at this in conjunction with 2928 because yesterday you told us that you had been appointed to -- as the consul general, I guess, for the Republic of Croatia to Venezuela.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, I was supposed to become an ambassador to Venezuela; however, since I hold dual citizenship, the highest rank that I could hold in Venezuela was that of a general consul. Since I had -- I have dual citizenship there, I am not formally an ambassador, and I discharged the duties of a general consul.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. And these two documents verify that; is that correct? The document that I showed you, 1D 02927, which is your appointment as of July 13, 1999, and we also see a translation regarding from the president of the Republic of Venezuela. So these demonstrate what you told us earlier, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see here both my roles as a diplomat in Bosnia-Herzegovina and now in Venezuela.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And the last document is 1D 02929, 1D 02929.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. This is a -- we have a -- I don't know, we can put this on the ELMO. This is what we received from the gentleman. It might be -- or pass it to the Trial Chamber. It might be easier for them to look at. This document here says that -- it's from the International League of Humanists for the Development, Cherishing, and Application of the Codex of Humanism and the Principles of Humanity. Could you please tell us who issued this certificate to you, when, and where?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the seven declarations and numerous citations I received, I treasured this one the most because here I was nominated a humanitarian by the international league -- in fact, of having been a humanitarian of the decade. Why was I given this --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When -- well, if you can just tell us when --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in Zenica, back in 1995, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And now if you could tell us why was it -- why was it given to you, if you know, and just be very brief because we have to take a pause.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to my strictly political role, strictly consular role, because I performed both - I had a political one, a political role and a consular role to play with regard to the entire population of Bosnia-Herzegovina - this document serves to show that I engaged in humanitarian activities in the situation in which Sarajevo and Bosnia-Herzegovina were in general. The people there required assistance. I spent two years in all, 1994 and 1995, in Sarajevo in addition to my visits there before. The situation there was appalling, as I describe it in my book, and there was a great need to assist the people there. I did so, as I was an ambassador there. It's enough to just glance at a map and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me if I interrupt you. But it seems that the document is at issue, and we should at least see it. We have a completely black sheet in our documents, and if you look at the ELMO where it should be, you have a black screen on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Where did this document come from? Because we don't have the original one, and I've seen it, but where is the original one, the original?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The original comes from the International League of Humanitarians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But where physically is it at this moment?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I copied this from a framed picture, but if the Court wishes me to present a much better English version of it, I can. I'm really sorry that it's turned out to be so poor --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But where is it --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the general consulate in Caracas --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We can provide --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have been shown the President's copy, which held against the light permits to recognise something. So I'm satisfied. We don't need to have the original flown in from Caracas --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I was just as concerned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- and the witness coming back. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Anyway, thank you very, very much, Ambassador Sancevic. I appreciate your testimony. I apologise for rushing you and cutting you off, and if I appear to be rude at times, my deepest apologies. But thank you very, very much, and I trust you will be equally forthright with the Prosecution or anyone else who asks you questions in this courtroom. Thank you very, very much again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are now going to break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Defence used four hours and 11 minutes. Witness, I don't have any specific questions to put to you, but I would just like one small precision which is an important one. At the very end, Mr. Karnavas asked you if you had read Mr. Tudjman's books. We had a list of the various tomes, and you said that you had been an ambassador in Bosnia and Herzegovina and you knew about his statements. Mr. Karnavas then asked you if you were well-informed sufficiently well in order to speak about Tudjman's policies with regards to vis-a-vis Bosnia and Herzegovina. You've answered yes, but you did not say what was the policy in question. So for the transcript, I would just like to ask a clarification, or rather, according to you what was Tudjman's policy with respect to Bosnia and Herzegovina? Would you be able, please, to perhaps finish your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I speak of the Croatian state policy vis-a-vis Bosnia and Herzegovina in general terms, since I was the exponent of that policy in Bosnia and Herzegovina. We often refer to the Croatian policy of President Tudjman; however, the Croatian state policy was not solely determined by President Tudjman. There were other elements there. For instance, the international community had a great role to play in all that. Then, for instance, the Croatian parliament. The Croatian republic is a democratic one. Of course, admittedly President Tudjman had a large influence to exert given the semi-presidential state structure. Still, I like to refer to that policy as the Croatian state policy with regard to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, what was my position with regard to President Tudjman on the one hand and the Croatian state policy toward Bosnia-Herzegovina on the other? Well, the two positions largely overlapped because the -- because President Tudjman took into consideration the views of the international community. Now, the federal structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina came across from Ahtissari, Cutileiro, and all the other players in that effort to find a settlement for Bosnia-Herzegovina. I for one played a part in that because I provided information not only to the government, the president of the republic, and the minister of foreign affairs, as well, on the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was complex throughout the time. It was an effort to take in and understand what was going on there, and my first and foremost priority was to be well acquainted with the Croatian state policy towards Bosnia-Herzegovina. In that, I believe I was not only well informed. I also -- and this did not -- the information did not only come from my conversations with President Tudjman but also [as interpreted] from his conversations with other figures, such as talks with Churkin and Petersen in Split, for instance, the important players that he spoke to from the international community. My role was to implement that policy, which was the policy of rapprochement as something that was only lateral. If you look at the map, you will see that for historical reasons Croatia embraces Bosnia-Herzegovina from three sides, and imminently there had to come a certain rapprochement. Ever since 1878, since the Berlin Congress, Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia were part of one state. First, it was Austro-Hungary; then it was the monarchy of Yugoslavia; then Tito's Yugoslavia; and so on and so forth. I believe I had a good grasp of it all since I was well acquainted with the history of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I have a library of some 6.000 books on Bosnia and Croatia back in Caracas. This is probably one of the reasons why Tudjman appointed me as the ambassador. I didn't have any sort of baggage. I didn't come back to Croatia before 1991. I came to Croatia, to Yugoslavia, for the first time in the month of August 1990. Let me answer your question in specific terms. I had to fully understand what the policy was, and I had to endorse it; I had to agree with it. I told Tudjman right at the start that if we should disagree that I would leave. Did I answer your question, or is there something else you would like to know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You've answered very clearly. I would have one additional technical question, very technical. We've heard many ambassadors here - I will not name them all - but as a general rule, when one is an ambassador in one country, one receives instructions from one's government, and then reports are drafted. So just a technical question. Between Zagreb and yourself in Medjugorje, were there any diplomatic telegrams sent back and forth giving you instructions, asking you to draft reports, and did you yourself, when you wanted or whether you were asked to do it or not, were you giving information to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs? This is a very technical question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Look, I already had experience in that. I did not send the same information to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs or -- and something else to President Tudjman. Whatever I wrote in the report to Dr. Mate Granic and before that I had another minister of foreign affairs who was Mr. Skrabalo, Dr. Skrabalo. This is how I addressed my reports, and this was governed by the constitution more or less to the president of the Republic of Croatia and the minister of foreign affairs, no matter who it was, Skrabalo or somebody else. So the wording was absolutely identical. There were no major differences there. This was very important to me. I found it very important that there was a unanimousness in the relationship vis-a-vis the president of the republic and the minister of foreign affairs. I wanted to avoid any possible confusion, and this was made possible by this procedure. Did I answer your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. I thought Mr. Karnavas was on his feet at one point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, on page 42, line 19, the word "only" is missing. It was translated that he did not come to the information from Tudjman but also -- and it should be that it did not come only from, so the word "only" should be inserted into page 42, line 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for this comment. Now, for the cross-examination of the other Defence teams, D2, I suppose. Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no cross-examination for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Khan. Mr. Kovacic, D3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave I would kindly ask you to allow General Praljak to put a few questions to the witness about book number 1, D 02808, about four pages in the book. The original pages are 124 through 129. This is a book by Dr. Sancevic. He is the author of the book, and these four pages depict four military maps, in other words, maps of military campaigns involving all the warring parties between 1991 and 1995. General Praljak, as you well know, is a soldier and he participated directly in these events. He has specific and special knowledge about that, and I believe that in keeping with your previous decision he is well-suited to put these questions because he's better equipped to do it than the Defence counsel. The witness has his own knowledge because the topic has been dealt with in his book, and we believe that this is an opportunity for us to introduce this part of the book into evidence. That's why we are kindly asking you to allow my client to put questions and confirm with the witness what he has already written in the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I shall consult my colleagues. Ah, I forgot the Prosecutor. Sorry. Please go ahead, Mr. Stringer. You're not a very difficult person, so that's why I sort of forgot you. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I should be more difficult. I was only going to offer the observation, Mr. President, that we've been provided by the Praljak Defence with the maps or the -- the parts of the book which I believe are the parts that they want to go into in cross-examination. And there is a lot of text -- I understand it's maps, but there is some text that accompanies the maps, which we don't have translations for. And -- actually, I could be wrong, and maybe as I go through this -- actually, counsel is indicating that I do have translations for this sections at the back, so I apologise for that. It appears we have been provided with the translations of those sections, and in that respect I would just add the Prosecution's previous statements in respect to Mr. Praljak conducting cross-examination. We would recall those at this time. Our position is that -- is as previously stated. At this point, we'll just respect whatever is the Trial Chamber's decision on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, with regard to relevancy, the Chamber would like to know - and I'm sure that you will be able to answer this question - the fact that these four maps on military operations would be shown to the witness with regard to military operations that took place between 1992 and 1995, what is the relevancy with respect to the indictment; and secondly, what particular point you would like to highlight when it comes to the questions that you will put. Would you be able to tell us this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the relevance of this book arises from the indictment, i.e., the alleged role of the Republic of Croatia and its plans, i.e., the policy of the Republic of Croatia vis-a-vis Bosnia and Herzegovina, and all this had to do with the joint criminal enterprise. These maps as a part of the military operations there point to the contradictions because this clearly shows contradictions with regard to the existence of the alleged plans and policies of the Republic of Croatia that the Prosecution alleges. That's the first point of relevance. The second point of relevance is an opportunity offered by the maps and the author who is sitting here to show the multi-layered nature of the developments and to show that there was an interaction there and that no single event in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the given period could be regarded in isolation, and particularly any military developments. I underscore that the witness himself has spoken about the fact that there was a multi-layered nature of the situation and that the situation had to be analysed within the context of its development. I believe that this is a good opportunity because we have a well-qualified witness, and this is an opportunity for us to demonstrate the context of all the developments which will allow us to look at the alleged joint criminal enterprise, particularly when it comes to the Republic of Croatia which allegedly participated in that, according to the Prosecution, and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, including its military leadership or the HVO, which was under the command of General Praljak.
