And I believe that this is the relevance. Maybe General Praljak has an additional idea, but this is what the two of us have discussed, and that's what we believe the relevance arises from.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could add one comment, which is this. I should have added this earlier. It's reinforced by what counsel just said. To the extent -- we're certainly reserving our objections in terms of relevancy but also in terms of the scope of the direct examination. If in fact what's being proposed now to go beyond the scope of the direct examination that was led by Mr. Karnavas, then certainly the guide-lines allow for that, but they don't allow for that in the context of an examination with leading questions. And so if in fact this is going to be a direct examination on something outside the scope of the direct by Mr. Karnavas, then I think we should recognise that for what it is and to act accordingly in terms of the procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Two elements, Mr. Kovacic. What you've told us - and I'm going to try to summarize it, and if I'm mistaken please correct me - you are telling us that this witness wrote a book, and four military operations, maps, are included there, and you would like to put question, you would like to ask your client to put questions, through which you would like to show that there was no joint criminal enterprise as defined by the Prosecution, and the best proof of this would be the military operations that abided to other ideas other than the joint criminal enterprise and that through the questions that you will put you will demonstrate this. And you would like to take advantage of the presence of this witness, who in his book mentions military aspects of this kind. The Prosecution objected to this to the Trial Chamber before deliberating, and I recall this on our behalf; when a subject was not raised within the framework of the examination-in-chief the -- of that accused, the other accused may raise this type of question, but the consequence of this is that you can only put non-leading questions and that the time that you will spend may be deducted from your general time. This means that if Mr. Praljak uses 30 minutes or one hour, the one hour used would be deducted from the total amount of time that you were given for all your witnesses. Did you understand me clearly? Mr. Praljak said "da," so he understood it clearly, I suppose. Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you have interpreted my intent perfectly well. I would just like to add an element a contrario of the allegation of joint criminal enterprise. The maps are just one of the elements a contrario; not the only one, mind you. Second of all, when it comes to your request for our explanation of whether this is a direct examination or a cross-examination, I believe this is a cross-examination for two reasons. First of all, during the examination-in-chief of this witness by the first Defence, the witness clearly spoke about the complex situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the enclaves and so on and so forth, about the multi-layered nature of the situation, and this is the segment that we want to deal with to demonstrate the multi-layered nature of the situation and more concretely to see the military aspect, i.e., the aspect of the war operations which were taking place in reality during the period of time that the witness was talking about. Second of all [as interpreted], the witness mentioned the events in Konjic, Usora, Posavina, Mostar, and so on and so forth, speaking about the specific events and the complexity of the situation. This is a sphere that we would like to tackle, and that's why we believe this is cross-examination because the topic was tackled already on direct and demands for clarification of the issues that were raised during the examination-in-chief, especially in view of the fact that the witness, a very qualified person, is the author of the book, and I will also say from my own information that this is a well-recognised book by the public. And he presents these maps in order to explain the thesis that he already raised during the examination-in-chief. That's why we believe that what we want to do is cross-examination and not just an additional examination-in-chief because the topic was already raised during my learned friend's examination-in-chief. When it comes to the calculation of time, we are talking about the different things. It arises from all of this that a cross-examination is a recognised and an acceptable tool to clarify matters and particularly those matters that were raised on direct. This is a traditional or the traditional definition of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. For the transcript, map number 22 relates to Usora. It is a topic that was raised by the witness. Map number 23 also talks about Usora, but we will now deliberate on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber deliberated and unanimously authorises Mr. Praljak to put questions to the witness, but the Trial Chamber will deduct the time of the questions from the time of the Defence of Mr. Praljak, and this is why Mr. Praljak should not put leading questions. He could again only put neutral questions, but I believe that Mr. Praljak understood this principle very well. Mr. Praljak, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for your generosity.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sancevic, Mr. Ambassador, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Before you, you have four maps taken from your book. Have you got the maps?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, yes. These are maps number 20, 21, 22, 23. Did you yourself draw these maps?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am the author of these maps.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you yourself enter the text under the maps, a description of the maps, as a key?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that is itself explanatory. An expert will understand the map without reading the text. A mere glance at a map explains a lot of things, but I myself can explain what I have drawn.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Today after all the experience that you gained in Bosnia-Herzegovina as an ambassador and as a person of knowledge, would you change anything in these maps as incorrect? According to what you know today, are these maps correct, and do they depict clearly what really happened over there?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me put it this way. There is always room for improvement, but I believe that these maps are valid even today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you very much for granting me these three minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you have no more questions. Thank you. I thought that you would --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I may have not been clear at the beginning, but I believe I was. We have a tool for introducing evidence. This is our door for introducing this piece of evidence. At the same time, we have a viva voce witness. We are aware of his qualifications, of his experience, and this is all that matters when it comes to the probative -- probatory value of evidence, and this was the whole purpose of this exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, another technical question. You were an ambassador, and as such you were knowledgeable about what was going on in the field. And as the Defence counsel have stated, the situation was very complex in the field. At your level, did you receive reliable information about military operations, or did you receive unreliable information? I'm talking about the time when you were an ambassador. Were you perfectly well-informed about the situation or not really well, or were you not informed at all about what was going on in the field? Can you please shed some light on this for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. First of all, I draw maps as part of my profession. I draw maps of the underground as well as of the surfaces above ground, so I am well qualified to my mind. On the other hand, in the embassy in Sarajevo I had a military advisor, General Daidzia. In other words, I could, based on the facts and on my knowledge from the ground, I could draw these maps. I don't know whether there are any other such maps apart from my own. I believe that there may be, but I'm sure that the maps that exist somewhere else should be compared to the ones here because these maps were drawn without any hidden agenda. Their sole purpose was to depict the real situation on the front line. I believe that in that respect, I cooperated with the UNPROFOR commanders, for example, the British commander, who were involved in the drawing of a similar map. So these maps are some sort of a synthesis of the military developments over there. There's one more thing I would like to say. I did not deal with military matters. I was concerned with political and consular matters mostly. However, these maps really represent the way things developed in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Your Honours, could I please try and go through these maps in a few brief sentences?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we're not sitting here to hear comments about these maps. My question was of a different nature. As an ambassador, were you well informed about what was going on in the field? That was my question. You answered partly, telling us that you had a military advisor, General Daidzia, who was in Sarajevo. Would I be mistaken in thinking that when you went to see President Tudjman to deal with various topics as we saw in the presidential transcripts, when you attended these meetings were you the one there who could - and, of course, there could be other people present; I saw that General Praljak attended some of them as well - but were you one of those who could shed some light on the situation for the president based on what you had seen, based on information given to you by your advisors, including General Daidzia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... when it came to the proposals of the international community. Maps were always on the table, the current situation as opposed to what should be done for the future. I participated in these talks about maps with President Tudjman and with other people who participated in all that, Dr. Mate Granic, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. I was checking the transcript, and I believe that as a result of my omission what -- there was not recorded in the transcript, the number was omitted, and the number is 1D 02808. It seems that this number was not recorded in the transcript. I suppose that it is my error or maybe a technical error. This really doesn't matter at the moment, but I believe that we should have this number recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we don't have any questions for this witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Tomic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Valentin Coric's Defence has no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 6D Defence has no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. The Chamber had given two hours to the other Defence teams. We'll therefore have some time for re-examination. Mr. Stringer, you may proceed with your cross-examination, and as far as you're concerned you have four hours and 11 minutes. And for once we are not really under any time constraints, unless, of course, the Prlic Defence decides to bring on Thursday the witness who is supposed to testify next week. Is that a possibility, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. As you can see, we need both of us to be in court. These are heavily documented cases. We need to go through the documents, and we try to be as efficient as possible. Next week's witness is going to take six hours to do direct examination, and we're still trying to decide how best to do all of it because in reality we would need at least eight, if not ten hours. So -- but the answer to that question is no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And before I begin, I can inform the Chamber as well as the witness. I won't be needing the map here, and so perhaps we could -- while the usher is in the vicinity we could remove the map before I begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And while that's happening, Mr. Ambassador, let me greet you. My name is Douglas Stringer. I'll be asking you questions on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm very glad to meet you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just a few questions, first of all, about your professional background and in particular, the time that you spent in the region of the former Yugoslavia after your return in 1991. As I understand it, sir, you returned to Croatia in August, I believe, of 1991 from Venezuela, which is the country essentially where you grew up. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct, but it is also correct that in August 1990 was the time of my first visit to Croatia as a member of the Croatian National Council in emigration.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And shortly, then, after you arrived back in Croatia this 1991, I think you used the word "seconded," that is, as a member of the home guard you were seconded to the Croatian Ministry of Information. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then at the end of 1991, about four months later or so, you were selected to be minister for emigrants, that is -- I've seen it also characterized as a minister for the diaspora. That's the next position that you held?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And do I understand correctly that, in fact, you replaced Mr. Gojko Susak, who was the minister of the diaspora before you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes because Mr. Gojko Susak could not hold two ministries. He concentrated on the Ministry of Defence, and then they were looking for a person to replace him in his capacity as the minister for the diaspora.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very good. And it was -- Mr. Susak had also been an emigrant who returned to Croatia when the war broke out there. Is that also true? He came from Canada, I believe?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So then he moved from being minister of -- for emigrants or minister for the diaspora to the Ministry of Defence, and then you took his position as minister of the diaspora, and that was, again, late 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. I said that Mr. Susak at one point held two positions, was in charge of two ministries: The Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of Emigration. He had to leave one of them, and the Ministry for Emigration was the one he left and concentrated on the Ministry of Defence. That's how the Ministry for Emigration position became vacant. They started looking for a replacement, and they came up with me. I don't know what the real reasons for that were, probably because I myself had been an emigrant.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then after that, then, in October or so of 1992, you became or you were appointed by President Tudjman to serve as a Croatia's first ambassador to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the date, jog my memory, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I have the appointment as taking place in October of 1992. I know that you didn't present your credentials to President Izetbegovic, I believe, until December of 1992.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that the procedure was this: First appointment, then approval by the Bosnian government, and finally I received my credentials, which I managed to present in Sarajevo on the 18th of December, 1992, and it was not easy, let me tell you. I travelled together with Mr. Izetbegovic, and we almost lost our lives on that journey. But if you're not interested in that, I will stop there. I won't go on telling you about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's interesting, but unfortunately we don't have the time to go into that. I think everyone recognises that the situation in Sarajevo at that point was very dangerous. I saw a report -- you indicated yesterday, then, that you remained in the position of ambassador until early 1996; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Because I saw a report, and it's not terribly important, but I saw a report indicating that in April of 1994 there was an indication that you were being replaced as ambassador by a gentleman named Andro Krstolevic [phoen]. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no clue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the report itself? If he's going to be making references to what he saw, I think common courtesy would dictate that we would be afforded with that report so we could see exactly what the gentleman is referring to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. President. It's -- we can distribute it. It's not among the binders, and it's not central. I just thought I'd get a clarification. The witness says he doesn't know anything about it, and so I think that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, if we're going to have any more surprises because -- especially in light of the allegations that we have been surprising the Prosecution, I would certainly request that anything that's not in the binders be not even -- be referenced unless it's already in the evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I can move on, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, I can refer you to one exhibit, Mr. Ambassador, which relates to sort of the next phase or the next position, if you will. You indicated that in -- I believe it was 1995 - you can correct me if I'm wrong - you actually then were elected to be a member of the Croatian parliament, the Sabor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was at the end of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And there's a document in the binders that I'd like to quickly direct you to on that. It has the number 10375. It might be in the second binder, but I'm not sure. What this is, it's just a press report of the BBC that is actually reporting on the election of yourself and others to the Croatian parliament at this time. We'll give you a chance to look at that, 10375. Yes, take a moment --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I believe behind it we should have a translation for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whilst the witness is reading the document, Mr. Stringer, a question. How come the name of the witness is highlighted in the BBC news report? Is there a reason for this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's because when we search open sources like the internet, you use a search term such as the name of the witness. And so when the documents, then, are found, they bear the witness's name in bold. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Ambassador, have you had a chance to look at that document?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Just a couple of questions about it because it's going to lead us a little bit into the next topic, which relates to the Croatian citizenship issue that you discussed yesterday. Is it true, then, that in late 1995, in this election, then, members of the Croatian people who did not live in Croatia were allowed to vote in Croatia's election?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And as I understand it, under the laws of the Republic of Croatia, then, there are a number of seats in the Croatian parliament that are actually set aside -- or at least at this point in time were set aside for members of the diaspora who would be elected to the parliament. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were candidates who could be elected depending on the number of the votes. I have to state that the persons eligible for the vote among the diaspora had to hold Croatian citizenship.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Of course. And there's an indication here that furthermore there was another requirement based upon the percentages of the votes that it was the HDZ special list -- there's a reference to the HDZ special list having won 90 per cent of the vote in the diaspora. So my question is whether those members of the diaspora who then took those seats in the Croatian parliament, were they all members of the HDZ party?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I can't tell you. I don't even know if I was -- let me see -- yes, I was a member of the HDZ at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Stringer. You have asked a question which has not been answered. Were there and do you know how many, if so, seats a priori reserved in Sabor for representatives of Croats living abroad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I must admit that I was only one of the candidates. Of course you know, it's only natural that a candidate may or may not be elected ultimately. That's the way democracy works. If I am elected, then of course I can relinquish my seat in the parliament and hold a different function. In that case, I would be replaced by someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The question was this, Mr. Ambassador: Do you know, as someone who was, yourself, a member of the Croatian parliament, within the Croatian parliament is there a number of seats in the parliament that are reserved for members of the diaspora? Do you know, or do you not?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that any seat could have been reserved, since that was a matter for the election.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, Mr. Stringer and Mr. Sancevic, for interrupting you, but I would like to say that the document which we are offered, that is P 10375, then 375, in other words, it gives an answer to the question which was posed originally by Judge Trechsel. And it says that in the last-but-one paragraph of that BBC news and information, it says that "In Zagreb Olujic told a press conference on Tuesday [14th November] who were 12 parliamentary members that would present Croatian citizens with no permanent residence in the Republic of Croatia. Only the special list of the Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ) can enter the parliament as it has passed a threshold of percentage of the minimum vote (5 and 11 per cent). The HDZ special list won 90.02 per cent of the vote in 'diaspora,' as 97.012 voters outside Croatia cast their ballots for the HDZ candidates." So for me it is rather clear that originally a threshold was established and only the HDZ special list could make it to reach that number and won 90 per cent of the vote. And that is why the 12 candidates had been elected by the expatriate votes abroad by the diaspora. So for me it is rather clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Ambassador Sancevic, I can move on quickly, but just to follow this or to tie this off, were you among 12 members who joined the parliament, then, after this election were people not living in Croatia, members of the diaspora, rather?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was elected.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you joined the Sabor, the Croatian parliament, as a member of the HDZ party; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but at a later stage. At the time of my election, I was still holding the position in Sarajevo. I had to relinquish the post of Ambassador to Sarajevo in order to take up my new duty. In the meantime, I had a person standing in for me in the parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That raises an interesting question. I think you said already you were a member of the HDZ party; is that correct? At the time that you were ambassador, were you a member of the HDZ party?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And were you a member of the HDZ party for Croatia or for Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, I was not a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I was a member of the HDZ of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then you left the position of ambassador to Croatia in Bosnia-Herzegovina. You then returned to Croatia in a different capacity, that is, as a member of the parliament?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I had my reserved seat in the parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you took your seat in the parliament, then, having never lived in Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I ask the relevance for all of this -- this line of questioning? Why is it relevant that he had never lived in if they have a constitutional process and they have rules of procedure in the Sabor that allows people from the diaspora to represent the Croatian nation? I fail to see the relevance. Now, I don't mind the gentleman wasting his time, but I do think that it is not relevant to the issues at hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, it's not a matter of relevance, but it's a legal problem we have here. Apparently, the diaspora was in a position to elect its own representatives, and 12 such representatives were elected. According to the laws - and we do not have these laws - are -- do the elected persons need to live in Croatia, or isn't it no obligation? Are you fishing for information now, or do you have that information, about their place of residence?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I think I have what I need on that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. You may proceed then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, now that the examination was interrupted. A discussion on a very specific solution of constitutional law and domestic legislation requires the technical knowledge and requires that we have the relevant texts of laws before us. If we shall embark on a discussion about a very complex piece of legislation which was in force in Croatia at the time and is not unknown to some other countries, if I may say so, we can't start this discussion by looking at a BBC news item, which is definitely not qualified to deal with this; and secondly, through this witness who did not deal with this matter in his examination-in-chief and is not a lawyer; therefore, he's not qualified to talk about it. We cannot engage in such fishing expeditions as this one because that's what I believe the Prosecutor is doing. This is not a serious approach to the matter. If the Prosecutor wanted to make some inferences on this basis, on the political impartiality of Croatia -- or rather, political partiality of Croatia and of Croatian policy toward Bosnia-Herzegovina, then he should have taken that other approach to the matter. It is, of course, in Their Honours' hands to decide whether to hear such evidence. Perhaps tomorrow we can call a waiter to discuss legal matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm not aware that any discussion has arisen. The Defence has raised objections, and I would like to invite Mr. Stringer to answer the pertinent question asked by Mr. Kovacic as to the pertinence of these questions of fact which you have addressed to the witness. That might be useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for allowing me the opportunity. In his direct examination - and this isn't all that complicated, or it certainly wasn't intended to be - in his direct examination, the witness said that he became a member of the Croatian parliament. The purpose here is simply to ask him about the circumstances under which he became a member of the Croatian parliament as someone who never lived in the country but who had nonetheless served as its ambassador. That's simply flushing out, if you will, testimony that came in the direct examination. And as I've indicated, I'm finished with it. I'm prepared to move on unless counsel wants to continue to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Ambassador Sancevic, I want to take you back to talk briefly about one particular period of time when you were the ambassador before we move on to the other topics. And in your binder, I want to ask you to look at an exhibit that's marked as 10393. Now, Ambassador Sancevic, you have before you the original text, which is a handwritten text. It's a two-page document. Perhaps you could briefly take a look at it to tell us whether you recognise it as your own.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise it, but you said that I never lived in Croatia, and that's not true. Let me refer back to what you said. I had lived in Croatia until I was 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. I stand corrected. You're correct on that. I apologise for having overlooked that. Now, getting back to this document, 10393. You talked yesterday a little bit about the many difficulties you experienced as the Croatian ambassador in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it seemed to me that this letter was a reflection of at least some of the difficulties that you encounter. So if I could, I would just like to take you through a couple parts of this letter. Do you recall writing this letter? It's a letter of resignation dated the 5th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you offered your resignation to President Tudjman through Mr. Granic, who was the foreign minister at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I note here that in the paragraph you marked as number 1, you're making reference to what you spoke about yesterday, your status or your attempts to be a stand-by ambassador or a roving ambassador was the word that you -- that came to us in English yesterday. Is that what you're referring to here in paragraph 1 of your letter?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The letter was written on the 5th of July, 1993, at the time when Mr. Mate Granic became minister. Until then, Mr. Skrabalo had been minister. During Dr. Skrabalo's tenure, I was a roving ambassador. The issue of opening up the embassy had not been solved. I had by then been preparing to open up the embassy in Medjugorje. However, on the list of ambassadors held by Mr. Granic, I was still a stand-by ambassador. That was my status at the time, and I wrote this by way of a protest. I told them, If you continue to list me as a stand-by ambassador, which is unfair, then -- but then Dr. Mate Granic and President Tudjman responded promptly by saying that it was an error committed by the administration of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. They offered their excuses, and I withdrew this request.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Just a couple of brief questions about this letter, and I'd ask if you could kindly - and I know it's difficult - give me brief answers to the extent that you can. There's a reference in paragraph 1 to opening an embassy in Mostar. Is it true that it was your wish to open the Croatian embassy in Mostar at or before this period of time, in July 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I was still looking for the best location for the embassy. When I told Mr. Izetbegovic that I should open the embassy in Sarajevo, he dissuaded me because he said that the great Serbs would destroy it. He offered that I should take Zenica as the location, and I looked into that possibility. Thereupon I considered a number of locations, one of which was Mostar; however, Mostar was faced with problems by then, and I gave up that idea and chose the area that was the quietest, and that was Medjugorje.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I believe you testified yesterday that then you set up the embassy in Medjugorje in August of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is that correct? I'm sorry to cut you off, but I've got some more questions and --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still have to clarify something. One does not open an embassy in 24 hours. You had to secure staff and premises, and when I mentioned the month of August, it means that I was busy trying to make sure that it is opened. And the embassy was operational to the extent that I have -- I had the number of staff that I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Then would it be correct to say that -- yesterday you spoke about the passport processing and the visas and the other certificates that the embassy was processing. Would it be correct to say that none of that, then, was taking place prior to the time the Medjugorje embassy got up and running?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. While I was a roving ambassador, we did not issue any certificates. I only had one driver who was by me, and that was all, and this was in the first half of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 2 of your letter, you make reference and you also make a statement at the very end of the letter. You're referring to your -- what your word is is: "Inefficiency and unscrupulousness in the personnel of our ministry ..." And I'm wondering, sir, was it a problem that your views -- you felt your views, as expressed in the letters you refer to here, your views were not being passed up the chain of command, if you will, or were not being acted upon in a way that you thought they should be?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not the case at all. The case of the matter was that a fledgling Ministry of Foreign Affairs, because it had been in existence for several years by then, was burdened by bureaucracy, which makes the operation of any agency difficult. I was a member of one of the most exposed ministries, and I had to be efficient. I was confronted with bureaucrats bothering me with a lot of red tape, and that is what I was complaining of in this letter. I wasn't referring to anything else. I was combatting bureaucracy because I had come from an area that was highly efficient, and I mean the field of oil industry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you. I'll take that answer and then move on. I have just a few questions on the issue of Croatian citizenship that you talked about yesterday in your direct examination, and now if I could direct you to -- if you still have the Defence binders, I'm going to direct you to the Law of Croatian Citizenship that you were looking at, which is Exhibit 1D 02918.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Ambassador, it's not in there. I think -- it's in one of the binders from yesterday, and she'll bring it to you.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I think you can proceed with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the law quite vivid in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. You were asked a few questions yesterday about determining who were the people who qualified as emigrants under Article 11 of the law. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Because being an emigrant is one of the bases by which a person can acquire Croatian citizenship under the law; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now -- actually, I'm looking at Article 3 here, which seems to lay out the various means by which someone can become a Croatian citizen, and the first is by origin, which I take to mean, who are your parents. You can become a Croatian citizen on the basis of the citizenship, if you will, of your parents. So that's one basis. Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then a second way is by birth, that is, someone who's born in the territory could also then acquire a citizenship in that way; and then thirdly, naturalization.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And naturalization is referred to in Article 8 of the law, and this relates to foreign citizens acquiring Croatian citizenship.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the basic article by which citizenship can be acquired through naturalization.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the question came up yesterday whether Croats who were living -- had always lived in Bosnia-Herzegovina, whether they were emigrants or not, and I believe your answer was: No, Bosnian Croats were not emigrants and therefore did not qualify under Article 11.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, look. It's not easy to explain this in just two words, but I'll do my best. Tell me exactly what you want me to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes. If I could walk you through the couple questions because it's -- I can assure you, it's not clear to me. This was my question on the Bosnian Croats, for example. If a Bosnian Croat wanted to acquire Croatian citizenship, would he have to do so through naturalization?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, because Article 8 is another basic article before you move on to Articles 11 and 16, which also deal with naturalization.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you actually anticipated my next question. Looking at Article 8, here it refers to foreign citizens. There are other parts that refer to Croatian citizens. And I wanted to ask you, if you could, to distinguish between what is a Croatian citizen as opposed to a member of the Croatian nation, which is referred to in Article 16. Is there a difference between those two terms?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, when it comes to definitions, definitions are not clear all the time as to what a nation is, what citizenship is, and what affiliation with a nation is. It's not clear across the board in all the nations. In that respect, I would like to tell you that I am inclined to adopt Professor Benjamin Aksin's [phoen] definitions. He teaches at the University of Jerusalem. He is very clear when it comes to these things. If you want me to do so, I can quote him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I -- let me continue to try to approach it from my perspective, and I hope it will get us there. Let me ask it this way: At the bottom of Article 16, there is a reference to people of the Croatian nation who would then submit their written statements to the diplomatic or consular office of the Republic of Croatia abroad. In other words, a member of the Croatian nation who's not living in Croatia may obtain Croatian citizenship if he or she meets the conditions of Article 8, paragraph 1, item 5; and if he or she issues a written statement that he or she considers him or herself to be a Croatian citizen. And then it continues that this written statement, then, is submitted to the competent body or diplomatic or consular office. So my question is: After you were able to establish the embassy in Medjugorje, were these written statements under Article 16 among the types of documents provided to you for submission in processing Croatian citizenship applications?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If somebody submitted all the paperwork in keeping with Article 8, then it was okay. If Article 8 could not be applied, however, then we had at our disposal two articles dealing with naturalization. The first one is Article 11 dealing with emigrants, and Article 16 dealing with the non-emigrant part of the population. And I believe that everything's clear there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Would you agree with me that Article 16 would apply to a Bosnian Croat?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, I would like to make a very clear distinction and issue a very clear statement as to how and in what way articles were applied. This was up to the Ministry of the Interior to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one moment, please. Ambassador, this issue on nationality is a very complex legal matter in a great deal of countries, but correct me if I'm mistaken. I have the feeling that you said in Croatia there was a mix of three situations: The right of land, the right of blood, and the right to nationalisation. The right of blood because a person is born in Croatia and that, therefore, person is Croatian. The right of blood, a person can be Croatian because their parents, the parents of that person, are Croatians or because their ancestors are Croat, and in that case a person that is in Bosnia and Herzegovina may be for two or three generations there, but they can say, My ancestor, my great, great, great-grandfather was Croatian, so through my blood connections I am a Croat, and therefore that person obtains a Croatian nationality. And the third possibility is the naturalization process. Through an administration process, a person may request to naturalization. So am I mistaken when I am describing this in this way or would you bring any correction to what I just said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that you are absolutely right. This was exactly the meaning of what I did as ambassador. We prepared documents. We received applications for citizenship as they were submitted to us. When citizenship was finally granted, it was up to the Ministry of the Interior to decide what article to apply. It was not up to us to decide which article would finally be applied at the end of the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, then, is it correct, then, to put it this way: A Bosnian Croat seeking Croatian citizenship in 1993 could achieve that either through naturalization under Article 11 -- sorry, Article 8 or could achieve it as a member of the Croatian nation who makes the necessary written statement under Article 16.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me put it this way. You are -- have been mentioning Croats all this time. Listen, my attitude towards Bosnia and Herzegovina is this: They were all citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina first and foremost. Therefore, irrespective of the fact whether they were Serbs, Muslims, or Croats, they were all in a position to apply for citizenship in view of this law. He could have hailed from Timbuktu, for that matter, and those people could also apply for citizenship. Whether they would receive it or not, that was not up to me. That was up to the -- as you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You have been asked about this law, so I think I'm entitled to ask you some questions about it myself, and that's what I'm doing here. Let me introduce another aspect of this that might possibly shed some light, and I'm going to refer you to your book, which is marked as Exhibit 1D 02339. This is the book that you wrote, and while the usher's getting that for you, again, it's 1D 02339. It may be that you don't need to refer to the exhibit since it's a book that you wrote yourself. Let me read to you a passage from the book. And I'm -- in terms of what's on the computer screen, I'm looking at the very bottom of this page which is currently up beginning with the words: "Immediately after winning the elections, President Tudjman begins to outline a new Croatian national policy ..." And, Mr. Ambassador, interrupt me if you'd like to take -- if you'd like to go to the parts of your book rather than me reading it to you, feel free to do so. But I'll just continue reading. " ... in line with the changed circumstances in BiH in the last 50 years, and pursuant to Article 10 of the Constitution of the Republic of Croatia that literally says: 'Republic of Croatia shall protect the rights and interests of its citizens living or staying abroad, and shall promote their links with the homeland. Parts of the Croatian nation in other states shall be guaranteed special concern and protection by the Republic of Croatia.'" And then you continue: "Hence, the Croats in BiH, regardless of the fact whether they are Croatian nationals or not, are guaranteed to be taken care of and protected." So would you agree with me that's what you said or that's a correct recitation of Article 10 of the constitution?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is based on Article 10 of the constitution, but since there's always some sort of confusion, you know, when we're talking about the first part of Article 10 as opposed to the second part of Article 10 of the constitution, I would like to define some things in order for us to understand each other better. I would like to define membership of the Croatian nation. A member of the Croatian nation is a person who identifies with a group of people who call themselves Croat. That's this affiliation or membership. However, in the first part of this constitutional statement a reference is made to citizens. If you are a member of a state, i.e., a citizen of a state, that state has to look after you just like I am currently looking after the Croatian nationals in Venezuela.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So I guess -- and that's ultimately where I'm trying to go. Dr. Tudjman during this conflict in 1992/1993, throughout the entire conflict in the former Yugoslavia, he was charged with the constitutional responsibility to look after the citizens of Croatia as well as Croatian nationals who lived outside of Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And that responsibility, then, is reflected, for example, in the Law on Citizenship, perhaps, which in fact provides a means or a vehicle for Croatian nationals to acquire Croatian citizenship even if they can't meet the other requirements, correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me, sir. I think they're injecting now a new terminology, "Croatian nationals." And I know that for a American, it's rather weird, but they're using the word "Croatian nation," so I think we need to stick to the same terminology. Otherwise, it's going to lead to confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's a good point. I'll try to use the word "citizens" for people who are citizens and "members of the Croatian nation" for people, perhaps, who are -- consider themselves Croatian but who are not citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, you can be a member of the Croatian nation and be a citizen of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's why I think we just need to be precise in our questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I think we are, Mr. President, but I'll continue -- I'll do my best. It is not a simple subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: My question, then, is whether this concern, this provision relating to parts of the Croatian nation in other states --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The best course is probably to have the break now. We're going to break for 20 minutes, and we'll sit until a quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. The hearing is resumed. Mr. Stringer, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, I don't want to linger on this too much longer, but let me see if I can just put a couple of last questions to you on the issue of citizenship and see if we can reach some sort of consensus. Would you agree with me, sir, that under the Croatian constitutional those parts of the Croatian nation, people of the Croatian nation - and I'm taking the word from your book - in other states, that is, living in other countries, that those persons were guaranteed special concern and protection by the Republic of Croatia? Would you agree with me that special protection applied to people who were of the Croatian nation living outside Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] That's what Croatian constitution says.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the same -- and since -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Bless you.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And since constitution is supreme law, if there is anything wrong in the laws which are in some fashion against what says constitution, well, bad for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's right. It's the constitution that's the supreme law?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, then, that this special concern or special protection is expressed to some extent in the Law on Citizenship in that the Law on Citizenship appears to make a special provision for members of the Croatian nation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. Before you answer that question. Excuse me. Now we're asking for a legal conclusion. He's asking him now technical questions on the law. The gentleman is not a lawyer. He's not a law professor. He's not a constitutional expert. I think -- if you look at the question that's being asked, he's asking for the legal opinion from a non-legal expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, counsel's asked questions of this very nature --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Ambassador Sancevic, you've heard the discussion. The Prosecution is putting a technical question to you. The Defence counsel who called you here objects. Please correct me if I'm wrong, but I believe I understand that a few a hours ago, you told us that you were very familiar with the issue of citizenship because you work as an ambassador and also because as a consul in Caracas you dealt with matters related to nationality or citizenship. Are you in a position to answer questions related to law or laws applicable to individuals who may qualify for the Croatian citizenship? Can you answer such questions or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can because I have an insight into the fundamentals of the constitution, primarily the constitution, and also into the fundamentals of the laws. There are laws that did not concern me, and I don't know anything about that, but whatever laws concerned me, the issues of passports, I had to know about those laws. But I have to admit, likewise, that it is not fair to treat me as a legal expert because I'm not a legal expert. I can read a constitution. I can read a law, but to dwell upon the essence and the substance of a law, listen, I'm not an expert in constitution or a lawyer, for that matter, as you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Ambassador Sancevic, if you do not understand the question, tell us so, and if you can't answer, just tell us that you can't answer because it's too complicated, but if you can give an answer, please do. Mr. Stringer, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And perhaps what I'll do, Mr. Ambassador, is simply read back to you the question that I asked before the objection. Would you agree with me, then, that this special concern or special protection which is expressed to some extent in the Law on -- I'm sorry. I'll start over again. This special concern or protection for members of the Croatian nation that is referred to in the constitution, is that concern and protection then expressed, does that carry over into the Law on Citizenship which appears to make a special provision for members of the Croatian nation in Article 16? So that's my question. The special protection from the constitution, does that flow over to Article 16 of the Law on Citizenship?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would put it this way. As far as I could observe, I saw no contradictions between the law and the constitution. That's as far as I could tell. How exactly the law was applied did not depend only on ambassadors and diplomacy but also the Ministry of the Interior, as I've already told you. In other words, everybody had a job to do. Did I manage to answer your question, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Not really. The word you used was "contradiction." Let me put it this way. It appears to me, would you agree, that there is in fact no contradiction and that there is in fact consistency between Article 10 of the constitution and Article 16 of the Law on Citizenship in that each of them relate to special -- each of them specially or specifically mention members of the Croatian nation?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] You are mentioning first or second part of the Article 10 of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm -- excuse me. I'm referring to the part of Article 10, I think the second part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am very calm, very reasonable, cold-headed, and in -- with my mind full I refuse to participate in this trial until it is determined what Croatia is guilty of or charged with. You are not asking me, Your Honours, to participate in this trial and to provide precise information about the military developments in a certain area. And what we are hearing here are attacks on the sovereignty of a state. As a member of this state, I refuse to participate, and I deny my counsel the right to participate. Please, sir. Please, Your Honours, just one more sentence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, I will let you finish. Because, you see, this morning I wanted to put that question to you. Last week, you took the floor quite energetically, and then Mr. Coric had the problem, we know. And at the weekend, I wondered why there was such a reaction, and I must tell you that I don't understand the problem. And what I'm expecting of you is to explain what the problem is. You have talked about this matter many times. Apparently, it's something that goes to your heart, but quite frankly I don't see what it's all about. Last time Mr. Scott put a question, you intervened. My intention was to review the transcript in order to find out what question had been put and what you had said precisely. Here, Mr. Stringer is dealing with the constitution, with various provisions of law. He's doing his job. He's asking clarifications from the witness about some issues, but now you take the floor, and you may be right, but I don't know because I don't see the problem, and you say, I refuse to take part in this trial. But please, can you very calmly - and you've told us that you were a quiet man - but can you tell us what the problem is exactly because I fail to identify it; I can't. Can you please very quietly tell us what is the cause for your reaction. Why do you react that way when we deal with these questions of law relating to whether someone is a citizen or not, why someone is a Croatian national or not? The witness told us that he was not the one taking the decision, that the minister of the interior was taking the decision. I don't know. We may have a witness later on from the Ministry of the Interior to shed some light on all this, but please try to tell us what the problem is. I'm ready to listen, so try to explain.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Antonetti, I will gladly do so. Why I said what I said and why I am simply not prepared for my mental and moral problems -- because I don't see them since, the meaning of this trial. Imagine a situation in which the French constitution was put for re-examination in order to re-examine the sovereignty of the French people or the Hungarian people or the confederation of the Swiss nation, The laws that have been passed in a legal and legitimate way, and then all of a sudden you find yourself in a war, in Algiers, in the Second World War, in the Iraqi war, and then all of a sudden you come here and you are completely calm. You are out of the game because of the bad legal system and process, and then you start talking about whether Croatia had the right to pass a certain law after 5 or 6 or 700 years of torture. Your Honours, French came all the way to Zagreb. Hungarians came all the way to Rijeka. Germans took whatever they wanted to take. Turks came all the way up to Zagreb, Sisak, and all the way to Vienna almost. And finally, when one people consisting of 4 and a half million individuals finally gets a chance to look after its own, then we get to a trial during which gentlemen from America charge us with things that are not applied to them. I am a professor of ethics and philosophy. I have been dealing with those things for 40 years, and I'm no longer able to participate. This is not even a farce; this is a burlesque. We have come here, at least I have come here, to respond to the charges before the law for my acts, for my doings, even for my thoughts that sometimes turned to words and possibly led to an act that was contrary to the law. But here things are happening that at the end of the day the whole of Europe is involved in what was going on in our area, And we're talking about the imperialistic mind. I can't accept that. You take the reigns in your hands and tell us what is legally founded in the Prosecution's examination. It is the constitution of Croatia? Is it the sovereignty of the people that is being accused at? is it the Croatian language that is being charged? I can deal with some counts of indictment, but this goes beyond all proportions. I'm here to deal with the charges, and I would like to share something very intimate with you. Just one more sentence. Your Honour, Judge Antonetti and other Judges, I really don't care whether I'm dead or alive, whether I'm going to spend 20 or 30 or 50 years here. There's just one thing that I've never understood. I've never understood those who accepted to participate in a rigged trial which led to their own conviction. I am here prepared to take responsibility for every act or -- that was committed or not committed but was supposed to be done. But we are now dealing with the farce or burlesque ^ which has no moral or ethical foundation. I'm not prepared to participate in that. I totally don't care how long this is going to take, 50 years or 100 years. I don't care whether I am alive or dead. Despite any grim prospects that may await me, I'm totally calm and cold-headed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor may wish to respond, but first let me sum up what you've just said. I think I'm beginning to understand why you intervened on many occasions. You seem to be saying that when the Prosecutor addresses the constitution or Croatian laws, he is challenging the sovereign right of your country to adopt laws in the field of constitutional law or nationality law. And you are saying that the Prosecutor is not entitled to criticise the Prosecution [as interpreted] or the law, and through the question he puts to the witness you feel that he's criticising the Croatian constitution and the Croatian law, because these laws were passed by your country in 1991, 1992, 1993 - I believe that's your position - and I'm beginning to understand what you're trying to say. I found it difficult at the beginning to see exactly what you were driving at, but I feel that I'm trying to understand -- I'm beginning to understand. You are, therefore, challenging the Prosecutor. He has the right to respond. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may, I do think it is also for the Chamber to answer. And I'm sorry to say, with all respect, Mr. Praljak, I think you are victim of a profound misunderstanding, a very profound misunderstanding. I have not heard anything which could be reasonably and for a legally trained mind could be regarded as a criticism of Croatia, not even of Croatian legislation. As I understand the debate here, and I stand to be corrected, of course, the question is how was the legislation conceived, how does it go together, what does it all mean, and how was it applied? And I suppose that in connection with the accusation of a joint criminal enterprise the Prosecution will try to establish that there has been some discrimination in application of the legislation with regard to people, members of the Croat nationality who were living in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is just an assumption that I make. That's how at the present stage I seem to understand the Prosecution. But I would like to assure you that at least for us in our view - and I would suppose in the view of the public at large - this is not an attack on Croatia. This is not an undermining of the sovereignty of the Croatian republic or anything of the kind, and I'm very sorry if you obviously feel, even personally, hurt by this. Take it from the Bench, and I'm sure that all my colleagues share this opinion, that in our view it is only a misunderstanding which could lead to the conception that there is anything attacking Croatia morally, legally, or historically in the actual discussion that we are dealing with. I think we've heard you, Mr. Praljak. I think we should give the floor back, as the Chairman has said, to Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I don't have too much to say in response. These are all documents that were provided as part of the Defence bundle for the direct examination, and that was my starting point. And these are all areas that were led as part of the direct examination; that's point two. I'm here on behalf of the Prosecution. I'm not judging, and I'm certainly not judging a country. I'm not questioning Croatia's sovereignty in -- nor am I questioning its constitution. However, I'm entitled to ask how the constitution applies to the laws that have been raised, how the Croatian constitution and the laws that affected the policy of Croatia, as it was exercised and implemented during the conflict. And that's where I'm trying to go, and I will continue to do that. I'm sorry if it offends people. I'm not intending to offend anyone, but the constitution says what it says, and the law says what it says. And I'm entitled to ask this witness to comment on all of these. He's clearly expressed his willingness to do so. So I'd like to continue with the Trial Chamber's permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please do. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And actually, Mr. President, I'm going to borrow a few words that were just said by General Praljak, who maybe expressed it even more succinctly than I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm certainly not questioning Croatia's history, the many events that ultimately led to the establishment of an independent Republic of Croatia. General Praljak just referred to that long history, and he made reference to, finally, the people consisting of 4 and a half million individuals, they finally get a chance to look after its own. And again, without judging, this is my question - I'm trying to ask it as neutrally as I can - that right or that chance to look after its own, that's what Article 10 as part of Article 10 of the constitution is about, isn't that true? Croatia looking after members of the Croatian nation wherever they lived.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to answer that? Yes. That is my response in relation to Article 10 of the Constitution of the Republic of Croatia. In other words, that Croatia shall look after members of the Croatian people. What more can be added to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In fact, then, when you went down into Bosnia-Herzegovina, isn't it correct to say that you as the ambassador were looking after the interests, and you concern yourself with the protection of the Croatian people who were in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, I'm sorry to interrupt you. I would like to have a follow-up question, and this question is related to a document which has already mentioned today, and it is a document which was submitted by you, by the Prosecution, and the number is P 00089, P 00089, and it is actually a presidential transcript about a meeting which was held on the 27th December 1991. I have to admit of course that you, Ambassador Sancevic, you have not been there, but there was the attendance apart from the leaders of the Republic of Croatia -- actually, the whole membership of the Herceg-Bosna leadership as it is put here, that is Mate Boban, Bozo Rajic, Dario Kordic, and Ignac Kostroman as secretary legal were there. And in that document you find in page 21, page 21, when Secretary Ignac Kostroman has actually introduced or rather informed the meeting about the session of Herceg-Bosna leadership. Then on page 21 in item 2, it -- he said and quoted, and I quote him: "The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna has once again confirmed the will of the entire Croatian people of Herceg-Bosna expressed on 18 November 1991 in Grude, taking the historic decision to establish the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which serves as a legal basis for the entry of these territories into the Republic of Croatia." And item 3 continues, and here I believe that there is a link -- the linkage between the territorial -- in a way, territorial policies and the -- and the question of the citizenship, and I quote here: "The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna recognises the full legitimacy of Dr. Franjo Tudjman as President of the Republic of Croatia and President of the Croatian Democratic Union to promote the interests of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna both among international factors, and during inter-party and inter-republic agreements on the establishment of the final borders of the Republic of Croatia." And I repeat the last part of this statement: " ... and the inter-republic agreements on the establishment of the final borders of the Republic of Croatia." Now, I would like -- my question is, therefore, knowing that you have not been there at that presidential meeting, if -- do you see any connection, any linkage between the issue of citizenship as contained by the Constitution of Croatia and of course the particular Law on Citizenship as well as between the relationship between the Herceg-Bosna community of Croatian people and the acceptance by the -- that actually the president of the Republic of Croatia is in a full legitimacy when he and Croatia, of course, promoted the interests of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna? So this is my question, and I would like to have your views about it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yet again, the notions of state relations and Herceg-Bosna are being misunderstood. I was a representative of the Croatian state and an ambassador to Bosnia and Herzegovina. I was not appointed as a representative of Herceg-Bosna. Herceg-Bosna was part of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I addressed at the highest level the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There was the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, within which there were certain elements we all knew existed. Second of all, it is not appropriate for me to comment upon what Mr. Kostroman stated here. Those are his views, and I have nothing to do with them. He was entitled to hold and promote whatever views he wanted. When it comes to the relations between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I do not want to enter into a discussion on these matters because I believe that they are beyond my competence. I would be interfering with the internal policies of Bosnia-Herzegovina if I started discussing these matters. You have to know that I was a representative of the Republic of Croatia, and as such I implemented the policies of the Republic of Croatia toward Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I do not wish to interfere with internal matters, matters that fall within the competence of Bosnia-Herzegovina alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, a question stemming from a question put by my fellow Judge that went to the heart of things. Judge Prandler just read an excerpt which shows clearly that on the 18th of November, 1991, the council, Croatian council was created made up of various territorial representatives. They are the ones who decided on the 18th of November, 1991, while Bosnia and Herzegovina was only recognised internationally in 1992; but these people decided to create this community. In the text, it is said the following, and I would like to call your attention on this very small paragraph, that it will be the legal basis in order for these territories to enter within the Republic of Croatia. So when we read this text, we may interpret this as being that the impulse came from these territories of Bosnia-Herzegovina, from these people who made this statement, and that they are the ones recognising Mr. Tudjman as being the president who will be able to put in place their deep aspirations. You were an ambassador in 1992, and I imagine that you must have met representatives of various municipalities. You may have even met Mr. Kordic, I don't know, but you must have met local leaders. Now, when you had contacts with these people, did you - yes or no, since my question is an open one - were you under the impression that this movement, Croatian movement in Bosnia and Herzegovina made more concrete by the HVO came as a spontaneous movement of Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and were they the ones without asking help of anybody decided to create this entity, or through contacts that you had with them there could be a different reason. What can you tell us? You were in the field. You were an ambassador there. You were perhaps in a very good position to give us your opinion on this matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, I said something that I had learned from the constituent statute of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and nowhere in that document are borders mentioned. I said yesterday that Herceg-Bosna never had any borders. I don't understand what it is that Mr. Kostroman referred to. He was referring to a territory and borders. I don't want to discuss this at all. If in 1991 the community of Herceg-Bosna was established - and we know the criteria upon which it was established - and if there were Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina who wanted to join, to be unified, with Croatia, well, then I can tell you that there were Serbs who wanted to join up with the Republika Srpska, and there were Muslims who wanted to join up with various Islamic organizations. Everybody is entitled to holding a view. I am not presenting you my views here. I'm talking about facts, and I'm telling the truth, which is what I'm required to do here as a witness. All I see is that this one Mr. Kostroman is expressing his views and his wishes. Now, I believe that I was quite clear in answering all the questions that had to do with the Croatian state policy. I personally, as a representative, as an exponent of the Croatian policy in Bosnia and Herzegovina, did not consider myself to be an ambassador on behalf of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. I represented one state with regard to another state. I can tell you openly that I never wanted to talk officially with the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna unless it had to do with matters concerned with the relations toward Bosnia and Herzegovina, otherwise it would have -- there would have been some other political motive that I would not have accepted. I was quite clear about my principles. The relations between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina were that of one independent state toward the other. Now, there could have been various internal developments, either with regard to the international community which put forth a number of solutions to the problems in Bosnia-Herzegovina which the Republic of Croatia fully endorsed or within Bosnia and Herzegovina internally -- well, of course I can tell you that there must have been individuals who held the same views as Mr. Kostroman here, and I would say that that was their business. I engaged in what was the official state policy of Croatia toward Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I thank Mr. Sancevic for his answer, but I do not want to continue this issue any further but only would like to state the -- actually to say that according to the records, the views which were expressed there, they were not the personal views of Ignac Kostroman, but as the transcript says, they were excerpts from the minutes of the 2nd Regular Session of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in expanded session with members of the BH HDZ Presidency, et cetera, and it was held on the 23rd of December, 1991, in Tomislavgrad. So it is what we are talking about and not about the individual personal views of Ignac Kostroman. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one last question to follow up on something that you said. Everybody will understand that you were the Croatian ambassador in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and we also understand that you presented your credentials to Mr. Izetbegovic.
